analysis.one_liner: Ends offshore tax loopholes, taxes fund managers' 'carried interest' as regular income, and limits stock-option deductions for corporations.
analysis.headline: The CUT Loopholes Act, aimed at raising revenue by closing offshore tax loopholes, never received a committee vote or floor action after being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets a set of tax breaks used mainly by large companies, hedge funds, and people with money offshore. It would let the Treasury restrict banks and countries that block U.S. tax enforcement, presume that offshore accounts in non-cooperative institutions belong to and produce income for Americans who control them, and require U.S.-managed foreign corporations to pay taxes as if they were domestic. It also taxes fund managers' 'carried interest' as ordinary income, limits corporate deductions for executive stock options, makes derivatives traders pay the standard rate on all their gains, extends the oil spill excise tax to tar sands oil, and tightens penalties on promoters of abusive tax shelters. Its stated purpose is to reduce the deficit so that important programs can be protected.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who pay their full share and rely on federal programs; the bill's stated goal is deficit reduction to protect those programs. Honest businesses and individual filers would face less competition from rivals that shift profits offshore.

how_it_helps.text: Treats corporations that are actually managed and controlled in the United States as domestic for tax purposes, closing the inversion loophole that lets companies relocate on paper while operating here.
Imposes new reporting rules and presumptions on offshore accounts and non-cooperative foreign institutions, making it harder for Americans to hide assets and income in tax havens.
Taxes fund managers' 'carried interest' as ordinary income rather than at the lower long-term capital gains rate, so investment managers pay the same rates on labor income that other workers pay.
Limits the corporate tax deduction for stock options to the value recorded when granted and applies the $1 million executive pay deduction cap to stock-option compensation.
Requires public corporations to report employees, sales, and taxes paid country-by-country, exposing where profits are booked versus where work actually happens.
Expands the oil spill excise tax to tar sands and similar oils and makes the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financing rate permanent, so taxpayers are less exposed to cleanup costs.

Stiffens penalties on promoters of abusive tax shelters, bans contingent fees for tax advisors pitching savings, and expands anti-money-laundering rules to investment advisers and company formation agents.
Treats all gains on section 1256 derivatives contracts as short-term, eliminating the 60% blended-rate discount that let futures and swap traders pay a lower rate.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that shift profits offshore, hedge fund and private equity managers, offshore banks and tax-haven jurisdictions, oil producers, derivatives traders, accounting and tax advisory firms, and companies granting large stock-option compensation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge funds and multinationals using offshore loopholes

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is real: country-by-country reporting, new account reporting, and expanded anti-money-laundering duties for investment advisers and formation agents add filing and record-keeping costs for financial institutions and companies.

The bill creates strong presumptions that offshore assets and transfers are controlled by, or are income of, the U.S. person involved, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence — a heavy standard that could make disputes harder for even honest taxpayers with complex offshore holdings to win.

Tightening rules on foreign income, intangible transfers, and earnings stripping raises the effective tax cost of operating abroad for U.S.-based multinationals, which critics argued could put them at a disadvantage against foreign competitors and encourage actual relocation rather than paper inversions.

Limiting the stock-option deduction to grant-date book value would raise taxes on companies that grant broad employee stock options, not just executive ones, potentially discouraging that form of compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The revenue and fairness gains are large and concentrated on those most able to pay, and several provisions (penalties for shelter promoters, oil spill excise expansion) are straightforwardly protective of the public. The main cost is compliance complexity and heavier evidentiary burdens in offshore disputes, which fall on financial institutions and on some taxpayers who are not evading. On balance the bill is a genuine deficit-reduction and enforcement package whose burdens fall on the wealthy and on corporations that had been avoiding taxes.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it, read it twice, and sent it to the Finance Committee, where it sat until Congress ended — it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Carl Levin introduced the CUT Loopholes Act on February 11, 2013, with Sheldon Whitehouse, to reduce the deficit by ending offshore and other tax loopholes.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
That was the final action of record: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a vote in the Senate before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, hedge fund managers, offshore banks, and tax-shelter promoters kept the loopholes the bill would have closed, and the potential revenue for deficit reduction was never raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals and hedge funds kept their loopholes

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so the partisan split was never tested; its two sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor is recorded.

industries.industry: Offshore banks and tax-haven financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would let Treasury cut off U.S. correspondent and card access for banks and jurisdictions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and would presume offshore accounts in non-cooperative institutions are controlled by and produce income for their American beneficiaries. Their business model of shielding hidden assets would face direct restrictions.

The Carried Interest Fairness Act provision would tax fund managers' performance fees as ordinary income at up to 39.6% instead of the 20% capital-gains rate, costing managers a substantial share of their income.

New rules on deferred foreign income deductions, intangible transfers to low-tax affiliates, earnings stripping, check-the-box, and offshore loans would reduce profits sheltered offshore, and country-by-country SEC reporting would make profit-shifting visible to the public.
Ending the 60/40 blended rate on section 1256 contracts means futures and swap traders would pay the ordinary short-term rate on all gains, raising their effective tax rate.

Penalties for promoting abusive shelters could rise to 150% of gross income and become non-deductible, contingent-fee arrangements for tax savings would be banned, and regulators would share enforcement information and examine financial institutions for shelter activity.

Expanding the crude-oil excise tax to shale oil, bitumen, and kerogen-derived fuels would make tar sands and similar producers pay into the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, whose financing rate would become permanent; the public benefit is a more solvent spill-cleanup fund.

industries.industry: Investment advisers and company formation agents
industries.note: Both would become subject to Bank Secrecy Act anti-money-laundering obligations, including suspicious activity reports and customer identification — duties banks already bear.
